Analytic compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} part II - one irreducible curve at infinity

Pinaki Mondal
Abstract.

We classify primitive normal compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} (i.e. normal analytic surfaces containing ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} for which the curve at infinity is irreducible), compute the moduli space of these surfaces and their groups of auomorphisms. In particular we show that in ‘most’ of these surfaces ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} is ‘rigidly embedded’. As an application we give a description of ‘embedded isomorphism classes’ of planar curves with one place at infinity. We also compute the canonical divisor of these surfaces; it turns out that their log discrepancy is related to the Frobenius number of the semigroup of poles along the curve at infinity. We use the computation to classify Gorenstein primitive compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with rational and minimally elliptic singularities, extending a result of Brenton, Drucker and Prins [BDP81]. As another application we characterize weighted projective spaces of the form ℙ2​(1,1,q)\mathbb{P}^{2}(1,1,q) in terms of their log discrepancy and index, generalizing a characterization of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} due to Borisov [Bor14].

1. Introduction

Normal analytic compactifications (henceforth to be denoted by simply ‘compactifications’) of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} are arguably the simplest, and consequently a well-studied, class of surfaces: see e.g. [Mor72], [Bre73], [Bre80], [BDP81], [MZ88], [Fur97], [Oht01], [Koj01], [KT09], [FJ11]. In [Mon16b] we studied singularities of these surfaces and of the curves at infinity (i.e. the complement of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}), and in [Mon16a] we gave an effective algorithm to determine the algebraicity of the simplest among these surfaces, namely those for which the curve at infinity (i.e. the complement of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}) is irreducible; following [Oht01] we call these primitive compactifications.

Combining results of [Mon16a] and [Mon16b] yields a description of singularities of primitive compactifications (Proposition 3.3), and in the case of algebraic primitive compactifications, an explicit description of the defining equations (Proposition 3.4) and the singularities of the curve at infinity (Corollary 3.5). In particular, all primitive algebraic compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} are weighted complete intersections and the curve at infinity has at most one singular point, which is at worst a toric (or monomial) singularity. Starting from these observations, we undertake in this article a detailed study of primitive compactifications.

The order of vanishing of polynomials along the curve at infinity on a primitive compactification of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} is a discrete valuation on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y], and it completely determines the compactification. The valuation is in turn determined by a finite sequence of polynomials called the key forms - these are natural analogues of the key polynomials (introduced by MacLane [Mac36] and widely used in valuation theory) of valuations centered at the origin. The key sequence associated to the compactification is the sequence consisting of orders of poles of these key forms along the curve at infinity. The notion of key sequences generalize the notion of δ\delta-sequences which are ubiquitous (see e.g. [Sat77, Section 2.1], [Suz99, Section 3]) in the theory of plane curves with one place at infinity. The main technical observation of this article is that under appropriate choices of coordinates on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y], the key sequence associated to a primitive compactification can be brought to a (unique) normal form (Theorem 4.6). Moreover, if the key sequence is in the normal form, then the automorphisms of ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] that preserve the key sequence or the corresponding valuation can be explicitly described (Theorems 4.7 and 4.9). Using these properties of normal forms of key sequences, we establish a number of results, namely:

  • •

    We show that the embeddings of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} in ‘most’ primitive compactifications are ‘rigid’; more precisely, if X¯\bar{X} is a primitive compactification of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} which is not isomorphic to a weighted projective surface of the form ℙ2​(1,1,q)\mathbb{P}^{2}(1,1,q) (for some positive integer qq), then X¯\bar{X} has only one subset isomorphic to ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} (Proposition 5.1).

  • •

    We compute the groups of automorphisms of primitive compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} (Theorem 5.2). In particular, it turns out that ‘most’ primitive compactifications, including all the non-algebraic ones, admit only finitely many automorphisms (Corollary 5.3).

  • •

    We explicitly describe the moduli space of primitive compactifications, i.e. the space of (isomorphism classes of) compact analytic surfaces of Picard rank 11 which contain a copy of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. The moduli space of primitive compactifications with a fixed key sequence (in the normal form) turns out to be of the form (ℂ∗)k×ℂl(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{k}\times\mathbb{C}^{l} for some k,l≥0k,l\geq 0 (Theorem 6.3). As an application of our result, we give a description (originally due in another form to Oka [Oka98]) of the moduli space of embedded isomorphism classes of planar curves with one place at infinity with a fixed δ\delta-sequence (in the normal form) (Theorem 6.7); in particular, the latter space is a quotient of (ℂ∗)k×ℂl(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{k}\times\mathbb{C}^{l} under an (explicitly described) action of (ℂ∗)2(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2} .

The remaining main result of this article is a computation of the canonical divisors of primitive compactifications in terms of associated key sequences (Theorem 7.2). This leads to a characterization (Corollary 7.7) of the primitive compactifications with rational and elliptic singularities and those which are Gorenstein. As an immediate application we recover the classification in [BDP81] of primitive Gorenstein compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with rational singularities (Corollary 7.9), and in addition classify primitive Gorenstein compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with minimally elliptic singularities (Corollary 7.10).

Two invariants of divisorial valuations (corresponding to curves at infinity on compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}) play a special role in this article: log discrepancy11 1 We follow [Jon12] to call it “log discrepancy”; it is called “K¯\bar{K} label” in [Bor14]. (Definition 7.1) and index22 2 It is called “determinant label” in [Bor14]; in [Jon12] it is defined, but not given any name; the motivation for our choice of the term ‘index’ is explained in Remark-Definition 7.3 (Remark-Definition 7.3). As an application of our computation of the canonical class, we give a characterization of weighted projective spaces of the form ℙ2​(1,1,q)\mathbb{P}^{2}(1,1,q), q≥0q\geq 0, in terms of the log discrepancy and index of the valuation at infinity (Corollary 7.4). As a special case we recover Borisov’s [Bor14] characterization of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} as (up to isomorphism) the unique compactification of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} such that the valuation corresponding to the curve at infinity has index 11 and log discrepancy −2-2.

It follows from our computation of the canonical divisor (Theorem 7.2) that the log discrepancy AνA_{\nu} and the index αν\alpha_{\nu} of a divisorial valuation ν\nu centered at infinity satisfy the following identity:

(1) Aν+αν\displaystyle A_{\nu}+\alpha_{\nu} =∑k=1n+1αk​ωk−∑k=0n+1ωk\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\alpha_{k}\omega_{k}-\sum_{k=0}^{n+1}\omega_{k}

where (ω0,…,ωn+1)(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) is the key sequence associated to ν\nu, and for each k=1,…,n+1k=1,\ldots,n+1, αk​ωk\alpha_{k}\omega_{k} is the smallest positive multiple of ωk\omega_{k} which is in the (additive) group generated by ω0,…,ωk−1\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{k-1}. It turns out (see e.g. lemma A.2) that ω0,…,ωn+1\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1} generate the semigroup of poles of polynomials along the corresponding curve at infinity. In the case that each αk​ωk\alpha_{k}\omega_{k} is the semigroup generated by ω0,…,ωk−1\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{k-1} (which is the case e.g. when ν\nu comes from a primitive algebraic compactification of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} and the curve at infinity is non-singular - see assertion (2b) of Corollary 3.5), it follows from a result of Herzog [Her70, Proposition 2.1] that the semigroup of poles is symmetric33 3 A sub-semigroup SS of ℤ\mathbb{Z} is called symmetric if there exists mm in the group S~\tilde{S} generated by SS such that for all s∈S~s\in\tilde{S}, s∈Ss\in S iff m−s∉Sm-s\not\in S. and the expression on the right hand side of (1) computes its Frobenius number44 4 The Frobenius number of a sub-semigroup of ℤ\mathbb{Z} is the greatest integer not belonging to it.!

In [Mon16c] we use the results of this article to classify 𝔾a2\mathbb{G}^{2}_{a}-surfaces (i.e. equivariant compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with the additive group structure) of Picard rank one and answer some questions posed by Hassett and Tschinkel [HT99].

We finish the introduction with a mention of one of the things not achieved in this work, namely a description of non-algebraic primitive compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} as explicit as the description of algebraic ones. More precisely, in section 3 we see that a primitive compactification X¯\bar{X} of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} which is not isomorphic to a weighted projective surface has a unique point P∞P_{\infty} with non-cyclic quotient singularity. The complement of P∞P_{\infty} in X¯\bar{X} is quasi-projective, and can be explicitly described in terms of key forms of the valuation associated to the curve C∞C_{\infty} at infinity (assertion (1) of Proposition 3.4). However, if X¯\bar{X} is non-algebraic, then unlike the algebraic case we do not have an explicit description of any neighborhood of P∞P_{\infty} in X¯\bar{X}. In particular, we believe that answer(s) to any of the following questions would be interesting:

Problem 1.1.

Assume X¯\bar{X} is non-algebraic.

  1. (1)

    Find an explicit description of the (analytic) local ring 𝒪X¯,P∞\mathcal{O}_{\bar{X},P_{\infty}} of X¯\bar{X} at P∞P_{\infty}.

  2. (2)

    In particular, describe when C∞C_{\infty} is singular at P∞P_{\infty} and the corresponding singularity type.

1.1. Organization

In section 2 we recall and introduce some preliminary notions and results necessary for the statement of the results of this article. In particular, we introduce descending Puiseux series (which in our setting are more convenient than usual Puiseux series for studying valuations centered at infinity), key sequences, and describe their relation with divisorial valuations centered at infinity. In section 3 we present basic results about singularities of primitive compactifications and the curves at infinity, and in the case of algebraic primitive compactifications, their embedding into (weighted) projective spaces. The results of this section are mostly reformulation or simple applications of results from [Mon16b, Mon16a]. Section 4 is the technical heart of this work; here we define the normal forms of key sequences, and state their basic properties. The proof of these properties are differed to the appendices, essentially because of the length. Sections 5 and 6 consist of applications of normal forms. In section 5 we establish the ‘rigidity’ of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} in ‘most’ primitive compactifications and compute their groups of automorphism. We use the description of these groups of automorphisms in section 6 to compute moduli spaces of primitive compactifications (modulo isomorphisms) and of curves in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with one place at infinity (modulo automorphisms of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}). In section 7 we compute the canonical divisor of primitive compactifications and apply it to characterize weighted projective spaces ℙ2​(1,1,q)\mathbb{P}^{2}(1,1,q) in terms of log discrepancy and index, and to classify (Gorenstein) primitive compactifications with rational and elliptic singularities. The main tool in our computation of canonical divisor is a result of Kuo and Parusiński [KP00] on multiplicities of Puiseux roots of polynomials. Appendix A collects some technical results on key forms that are used throughout the article. The remaining four appendices are devoted to the proof of the properties of normal forms stated in section 4. In particular, we study in appendix B the effect of changes of the coefficients of a descending Puiseux series on the associated key forms, and in appendix C the effect of change of coordinates on ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} on the coefficients of a descending Puiseux series. Finally, in appendices D and E we combine these results to prove the properties of key forms.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Divisorial semidegrees and descending Puiseux series

Let X¯(x,y)\bar{X}_{(x,y)} be a copy of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} such that X:=ℂ2X:=\mathbb{C}^{2} is embedded into X¯(x,y)\bar{X}_{(x,y)} via the map (x,y)↦[1:x:y](x,y)\mapsto[1:x:y].

Definition 2.1 (Divisorial discrete valuations).

A discrete valuation on ℂ⁡(x,y)\mathbb{C}(x,y) is a map ν:ℂ⁡(x,y)∖{0}→ℤ\nu:\mathbb{C}(x,y)\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{Z} such that for all f,g∈ℂ⁡(x,y)∖{0}f,g\in\mathbb{C}(x,y)\setminus\{0\},

  • •

    ν⁡(f+g)≥min⁡{ν⁡(f),ν⁡(g)}\nu(f+g)\geq\min\{\nu(f),\nu(g)\},

  • •

    ν⁡(f​g)=ν⁡(f)+ν⁡(g)\nu(fg)=\nu(f)+\nu(g).

A discrete valuation ν\nu on ℂ⁡(x,y)\mathbb{C}(x,y) is called divisorial iff there exists a normal algebraic surface YνY_{\nu} equipped with a birational map σ:Yν→X¯(x,y)\sigma:Y_{\nu}\to\bar{X}_{(x,y)} and a curve CνC_{\nu} on YνY_{\nu} such that for all non-zero f∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in\mathbb{C}[x,y], ν⁡(f)\nu(f) is the order of vanishing of σ∗​(f)\sigma^{*}(f) along CνC_{\nu}. The center of ν\nu on X¯(x,y)\bar{X}_{(x,y)} is σ⁡(Cν)\sigma(C_{\nu}). ν\nu is said to be centered at infinity (on X¯(x,y)\bar{X}_{(x,y)}) iff the center of ν\nu on X¯(x,y)\bar{X}_{(x,y)} is contained in X¯(x,y)∖X\bar{X}_{(x,y)}\setminus X; equivalently, ν\nu is centered at infinity iff there is a non-zero polynomial f∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] such that ν⁡(f)<0\nu(f)<0.

Definition 2.2 (Divisorial semidegrees).

A divisorial semidegree on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] is a map δ:ℂ⁡(x,y)∖{0}→ℤ\delta:\mathbb{C}(x,y)\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{Z} such that −δ-\delta is a divisorial discrete valuation centered at infinity.

The field of descending Puiseux series in xx is

2.2. Key sequences and key forms

Remark 2.9.

Let ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be a key sequence. Definition 2.10 (Key forms).

Let ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be a key sequence and θ→:=(θ1,…,θn)∈(ℂ∗)n\vec{\theta}:=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n})\in(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}. The corresponding key forms are elements g0,…,gn+1g_{0},\ldots,g_{n+1} in ℂ⁡[x,x−1,y]\mathbb{C}[x,x^{-1},y] defined as follows: g0:=xg_{0}:=x, g1:=yg_{1}:=y, and

gk+1=gkαk−θkg0βk,0⋯gk−1βk,k−1,1≤k≤n,\displaystyle g_{k+1}=g_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}-\theta_{k}g_{0}^{\beta_{k,0}}\cdots g_{k-1}^{\beta_{k,k-1}},\quad 1\leq k\leq n,

where αk\alpha_{k}’s and βk,j\beta_{k,j}’s are as in Remark 2.9.

Key forms are clear-cut analogues of the notion of key polynomials corresponding to discrete valuations introduced by MacLane [Mac36]. It follows from the standard theory of discrete valuations (as developed in e.g. [FJ04, Chapters 2, 4]) that there are pairwise correspondences among the following families:

  1. (A)

    Pairs (ω→,θ→)(\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}) where ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) is a key sequence and θ→:=(θ1,…,θn)∈(ℂ∗)n\vec{\theta}:=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n})\in(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}.

  2. (B)

    Divisorial semidegrees δ\delta on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] such that δ⁡(x)>0\delta(x)>0.

  3. (C)

    Pairs (ϕ,r)(\phi,r) where ϕ\phi is a descending Puiseux polynomial, i.e. an element of ℂ​⟨⟨x⟩⟩{\mathbb{C}}\langle\langle x\rangle\rangle with finitely many terms, r∈ℚr\in\mathbb{Q}, r<ordx⁡(ϕ)r<\ord_{x}(\phi).

The correspondence between (B) and (C) is given by Proposition 2.4. The mapping (ω,θ)↦δω→,θ→(\omega,\theta)\mapsto\delta_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} defined in Theorem 2.11 below gives the correspondence (A) →\to (B).

Theorem 2.11.

Let (ω→,θ→)(\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}) be as in (A), y1,…,yn+1y_{1},\ldots,y_{n+1} be indeterminates and ω\omega be the weighted degree on S:=ℂ⁡[x,x−1,y1,…,yn+1]S:=\mathbb{C}[x,x^{-1},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n+1}] corresponding to weights ω0\omega_{0} for xx and ωj\omega_{j} for yjy_{j}, 0≤j≤n+10\leq j\leq n+1 (i.e. the value of ω\omega on a polynomial is the maximum ‘weight’ of its monomials). For every polynomial f∈ℂ⁡[x,x−1,y]f\in\mathbb{C}[x,x^{-1},y], define

(4) δ(f):=min{ω(F):F(x,y1,…,yn+1)∈S,F(g0,g1,…,gn+1)=f}.\displaystyle\delta(f):=\min\{\omega(F):F(x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{n+1})\in S,\ F(g_{0},g_{1},\ldots,g_{n+1})=f\}.

where g0,…,gn+1g_{0},\ldots,g_{n+1} are key forms corresponding to (ω→,θ→)(\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}). Then δ\delta is a divisorial semidegree on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] such that δ⁡(gk)=ωk\delta(g_{k})=\omega_{k}, 0≤k≤n+10\leq k\leq n+1; in particular, δ⁡(x)=ω0>0\delta(x)=\omega_{0}>0.

Proof.

Follows from [Mon16a, Theorem 3.17]. ∎

Combining Theorem 2.11 with Proposition 2.4 gives the correspondence (A) →\to (C). The correspondence (C) →\to (A) is described in detail in [Mon16a, Algorithm 5.1]; we summarize it below.

Remark 2.14.

δ\delta-sequences of plane curves with one place at infinity are special cases of key sequences; e.g. the definition of δ\delta-sequences in [Sat77, p. 1116] is equivalent to the following definition: a sequence ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}), n∈ℤ≥0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, of integers is a δ\delta-sequence if it is a primitive algebraic key sequence such that

  • •

    αk≥2\alpha_{k}\geq 2 for k=2,…,nk=2,\ldots,n. In other words, the essential subsequence of ω→\vec{\omega} is either ω→\vec{\omega} or (ω0,ω2,ω3,…,ωn+1)(\omega_{0},\omega_{2},\omega_{3},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}).

  • •

    αn+1​ωn+1∈ℤ≥0​⟨ω0,…,ωn⟩\alpha_{n+1}\omega_{n+1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\langle\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n}\rangle, i.e. the identity from property (4) of primitive algebraic key sequences holds for k=n+1k=n+1 as well.

Geometrically the relation between δ\delta-sequences of plane curves and key sequences of semidegrees can be seen in the following way: let C=V⁡(f)⊆ℂ2C=V(f)\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} be a curve with one place at infinity, where f∈ℂ⁡[x,y]f\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] is an irreducible polynomial. Let Cξ:=V⁡(f−ξ)⊆ℂ2C_{\xi}:=V(f-\xi)\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} for each ξ∈ℂ\xi\in\mathbb{C}. It is a classical result of Moh [Moh74] that each CξC_{\xi} has one place at infinity, call it PξP_{\xi}. Let δC\delta_{C} be the semidegree on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] that assigns to each h∈ℂ⁡[x,y]h\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] the order of pole at PξP_{\xi} of h|Cξh|_{C_{\xi}} for generic ξ\xi. Let ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be the key sequence of δC\delta_{C} and ω→e:=(ωi0,…,ωil+1)\vec{\omega}_{e}:=(\omega_{i_{0}},\ldots,\omega_{i_{l+1}}) be its essential subsequence, where 0=i0<⋯<il+1=n+10=i_{0}<\cdots<i_{l+1}=n+1. Then ωil+1=0\omega_{i_{l+1}}=0, and the δ\delta-sequence of CC in (x,y)(x,y)-coordinates is:

(5) d→:={(ωi0,…,ωil)if​i1=1,(ωi0,ω1,ωi2,…,ωil)if​i1>1.\displaystyle\vec{d}:=\begin{cases}(\omega_{i_{0}},\ldots,\omega_{i_{l}})&\text{if}\ i_{1}=1,\\ (\omega_{i_{0}},\omega_{1},\omega_{i_{2}},\ldots,\omega_{i_{l}})&\text{if}\ i_{1}>1.\end{cases}

3. Basic structure of primitive compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}

Notation 3.1.

Let (x,y)(x,y) be a fixed system of coordinates on X:=ℂ2X:=\mathbb{C}^{2}. Let ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be a key sequence, θ→:=(θ1,…,θn)∈(ℂ∗)n\vec{\theta}:=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n})\in(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}, and δω→,θ→\delta_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} be the associated semidegree on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] as in Theorem 2.11. In case δω→,θ→\delta_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} is primitive (Definition 2.6), we write X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} for the corresponding primitive compactification of XX.

Theorem 3.2.

  1. (1)

    δω→,θ→\delta_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} is primitive iff ω→\vec{\omega} is primitive.

  2. (2)

    Assume δω→,θ→\delta_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} is primitive. Then X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} is algebraic iff ω→\vec{\omega} is algebraic.

Proof.

The first assertion is a reformulation of [Mon16b, Corollary 6.3]. The second assertion follows from [Mon16a, Theorem 4.1]. ∎

[Mon16b, Theorem 4.5] gives an explicit description of dual graphs of minimal resolutions of singularities of primitive compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. Proposition 3.3 below collects some information about the singularities of primitive compactifications and the curves on infinity on these surfaces; it follows in a straightforward manner from an examination of these dual graphs.

Proposition 3.3.

Let ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be a primitive key sequence and θ→∈(ℂ∗)n\vec{\theta}\in(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}. Let X¯:=X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}:=\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}, C∞C_{\infty} be the curve at infinity on X¯\bar{X}, and P∞∈C∞P_{\infty}\in C_{\infty} be as in Proposition 2.7.

  1. (1)

    X¯\bar{X} has at most two singular points.

    1. (a)

      If X¯\bar{X} is isomorphic to a weighted projective surface of the form ℙ2​(1,p,q)\mathbb{P}^{2}(1,p,q), with 1≤p≤q1\leq p\leq q, then

      1. (i)

        If p=qp=q, then X¯≅ℙ2\bar{X}\cong\mathbb{P}^{2} and therefore X¯\bar{X} is nonsingular.

      2. (ii)

        Otherwise let p′:=p/gcd⁡(p,q)p^{\prime}:=p/\gcd(p,q) and q′:=q/gcd⁡(p,q)q^{\prime}:=q/\gcd(p,q). If p′=1p^{\prime}=1, then X¯\bar{X} has only one singular point, which is a cyclic quotient singularity66 6 Let PP be an isolated singular point on a surface UU, and a,b,ca,b,c be positive integers. Then UU is said to have a cyclic quotient singularity at PP of type 1a​(b,c)\frac{1}{a}(b,c) iff PP has a neighborhood in UU isomorphic to a neighborhood of the origin in the quotient of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} under the action of the group of aa-th roots of unity given by ζ⋅(u,v)=(ζb​u,ζc​v)\zeta\cdot(u,v)=(\zeta^{b}u,\zeta^{c}v), where ζ\zeta is a primitive aa-th root of unity. of type 1q′​(1,1)\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}(1,1).

      3. (iii)

        Otherwise X¯\bar{X} has two singular points, both cyclic quotient singularities, one of type 1q′​(1,p′)\frac{1}{q^{\prime}}(1,p^{\prime}) and the other of type 1p′​(1,q′)\frac{1}{p^{\prime}}(1,q^{\prime}).

    2. (b)

      Otherwise X¯\bar{X} has a non-cyclic quotient singularity at P∞P_{\infty}. Let ω′:=gcd⁡(ω0,…,ωn)\omega^{\prime}:=\gcd(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n}).

      1. (i)

        If ω′=1\omega^{\prime}=1, then X¯\bar{X} has no other singular points, i.e. Sing⁡(X¯)={P∞}\sing(\bar{X})=\{P_{\infty}\}.

      2. (ii)

        Otherwise X¯\bar{X} has precisely one singular point P0P_{0} other than P∞P_{\infty}. P0P_{0} is a cyclic quotient singularity of type 1ω′​(1,ωn+1)\frac{1}{\omega^{\prime}}(1,\omega_{n+1}).

  2. (2)

    C∞C_{\infty} is non-singular off P∞P_{\infty}. In particular C∞∖P∞≅ℂC_{\infty}\setminus P_{\infty}\cong\mathbb{C}. Moreover, in case (1a), C∞C_{\infty} is non-singular, i.e. C∞≅ℙ1C_{\infty}\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}. ∎

Our next result is about embeddings of primitive compactifications X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} into projective spaces. If X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} is not algebraic, then of course such embeddings do not exist. However, X¯ω→,θ→∖{P∞}\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}\setminus\{P_{\infty}\} (where P∞P_{\infty} is as in Proposition 3.3) remains a quasi-projective variety (since X¯ω→,θ→∖{P∞}\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}\setminus\{P_{\infty}\} is either non-singular or has only one rational singular point, and therefore is quasi-projective due to the algebraicity criterion of Artin [Art62]). In particular, X¯ω→,θ→∖V⁡(x)\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}\setminus V(x) (where V⁡(x)V(x) is the closure of the yy-axis) is quasi-projective (since Proposition 2.7 implies that P∞∈V⁡(x)P_{\infty}\in V(x)). The first part of the next proposition shows that X¯ω→,θ→∖V⁡(x)\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}\setminus V(x) is in fact an affine surface, with a closed embedding defined by the key forms of δω→,θ→\delta_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}. In the case that X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} is algebraic, the embedding extends to all of X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}, and realizes it as a weighted complete intersection in a weighted projective space, whose defining equations can be explicitly described.

Proposition 3.4.

Let ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be a key sequence and θ→∈(ℂ∗)n\vec{\theta}\in(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{n}. Let g0,…,gn+1g_{0},\ldots,g_{n+1} be the key forms associated to (ω→,θ→)(\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}) and 𝐖​ℙ{\bf W}\mathbb{P} be the weighted projective space ℙn+2​(1,ω0,ω1,…,ωn+1)\mathbb{P}^{n+2}(1,\omega_{0},\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) with (weighted) homogeneous coordinates [w:y0:⋯:yn+1][w:y_{0}:\cdots:y_{n+1}].

  1. (1)

    The map ιω→,θ→:X∖V⁡(x)↪𝐖​ℙ∖V⁡(y0)\iota_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}:X\setminus V(x)\hookrightarrow{\bf W}\mathbb{P}\setminus V(y_{0}) given by

    (x,y)↦[1:g0(x,y):g1(x,y):⋯:gn+1(x,y)]\displaystyle(x,y)\mapsto[1:g_{0}(x,y):g_{1}(x,y):\cdots:g_{n+1}(x,y)]

    induces an open embedding of X∖V⁡(x)X\setminus V(x) into the closure YY in 𝐖​ℙ∖V⁡(y0){\bf W}\mathbb{P}\setminus V(y_{0}) of its image. The complement CC of X∖V⁡(x)X\setminus V(x) in YY is isomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C} and the order of pole along CC is precisely δω→,θ→\delta_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}. If ω→\vec{\omega} is primitive, then Y≅X¯ω→,θ→∖V⁡(x)Y\cong\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}\setminus V(x).

  2. (2)

    If ω→\vec{\omega} is primitive algebraic, then ιω→,θ→\iota_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} induces an isomorphism of X¯ω→,θ→\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}} with the subvariety of 𝐖​ℙ{\bf W}\mathbb{P} defined by weighted homogeneous polynomials GkG_{k}, 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, given by

    (6) Gk:=wαk​ωk−ωk+1​yk+1−(ykαk−θk​∏j=0k−1yjβk,j)\displaystyle G_{k}:=w^{\alpha_{k}\omega_{k}-\omega_{k+1}}y_{k+1}-\left(y_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}-\theta_{k}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}y_{j}^{\beta_{k,j}}\right)

    where αk\alpha_{k}’s and βk,j\beta_{k,j}’s are as in Remark 2.9.

Proof.

The first assertion is a consequence of lemma A.2, and the second of [Mon16a, Theorem 4.1]. ∎

    1. (a)

    2. (b)

Remark 3.6.

  1. (a)

    P0P_{0} and P∞P_{\infty} of Corollary 3.5 are the same as P0P_{0} and P∞P_{\infty} from Proposition 3.3.

Proof of Corollary 3.5.

Since C∞=V⁡(w)∩X¯ω→,θ→C_{\infty}=V(w)\cap\bar{X}_{\vec{\omega},\vec{\theta}}, Proposition 3.4 implies that

The index of a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-Cartier divisor DD is the smallest positive integer mm such that m​DmD is Cartier. The following result describes the index of the divisor at infinity on a primitive algebraic compactification.

Proposition 3.7.

Let ω→\vec{\omega} and C∞C_{\infty} be as in Corollary 3.5. Then the index of [C∞][C_{\infty}] is αn+1​ωn+1\alpha_{n+1}\omega_{n+1}, where αn+1:=gcd⁡(ω0,…,ωn)\alpha_{n+1}:=\gcd(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n}) and [C∞][C_{\infty}] is the Weil divisor corresponding to C∞C_{\infty}.

Proof.

4. Normal forms of key sequences

In this section we introduce normal forms of key sequences associated with divisorial semidegrees, and state their basic properties. The proofs of these properties are in appendices D and E. We start with some examples which motivate the definition of normal forms.

4.2. Basic properties of normal forms

The results in this section state the fundamental properties of normal forms. The proofs of Theorems 4.6 and 4.7 are in appendix D and the proof of Theorem 4.9 is in appendix E.

Let X:=ℂ2X:=\mathbb{C}^{2} and δ\delta be a divisorial semidegree on ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X]. Then

5. Automorphisms of primitive compactifications

Our first application of normal forms is the ‘rigidity’ of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} in a primitive compactification:

Proposition 5.1.

Let X¯\bar{X} be a primitive compactification of X:=ℂ2X:=\mathbb{C}^{2}. Let UU be an (open) subset of X¯\bar{X} isomorphic to ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}.

  1. (1)

Corollary 5.3.

Adopt the notations of Theorem 5.2. If kX¯≥−1k_{\bar{X}}\geq-1 and n≥2n\geq 2, then X¯\bar{X} admits only finitely many automorphisms. In particular, every non-algebraic primitive compactification of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} admits only finitely many automorphisms.

The first statement follows from assertion (2) of Theorem 5.2. For the last statement, we show that if X¯\bar{X} is non-algebraic, then kX¯>−1k_{\bar{X}}>-1 and n≥2n\geq 2. Indeed, if kX¯≤−1k_{\bar{X}}\leq-1, then Corollary 7.7 implies that X¯\bar{X} has only rational singularities, so that Artin’s contraction criterion [Art66] implies that X¯\bar{X} is algebraic. On the other hand, if n≤1n\leq 1, then it is straightforward to see that ω→\vec{\omega} is an algebraic key sequence, so that X¯\bar{X} is algebraic (Theorem 3.2). ∎

6. Moduli spaces

In this section we compute moduli spaces of two kinds of objects:

  • •

    primitive normal compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} modulo isomorphisms (in the category of normal analytic surfaces), and

  • •

    curves C⊆ℂ2C\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{2} with one place at infinity modulo automorphisms of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}.

Definition 6.1.

Let ω→\vec{\omega} be a primitive key sequence in normal form. We denote by 𝒴ω→\mathcal{Y}_{\vec{\omega}} the moduli space of primitive normal compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with key sequence ω→\vec{\omega}. More precisely, 𝒴ω→\mathcal{Y}_{\vec{\omega}} is the set of (isomorphism classes of) compact normal analytic surfaces YY of Picard rank 11 such that

  1. (1)

    YY has a subset XX isomorphic to ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, and

  2. (2)

    if δ\delta is the semidegree on ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X] corresponding to C∞:=Y∖XC_{\infty}:=Y\setminus X, then there exists a system of coordinates (x,y)(x,y) on XX such that δ⁡(x)>0\delta(x)>0 and ω→\vec{\omega} is the key sequence of δ\delta in (x,y)(x,y) coordinates.

In case that ω→\vec{\omega} is also an essential key sequence, we denote by 𝒴ω→e\mathcal{Y}^{e}_{\vec{\omega}} the union of all 𝒴ω→′\mathcal{Y}_{\vec{\omega}^{\prime}} such that

  1. (3)

    ω→′\vec{\omega}^{\prime} is a primitive key sequence in normal form, and

  2. (4)

    the essential subsequence of ω→′\vec{\omega}^{\prime} is ω→\vec{\omega}.

Finally 𝒴ω→e,a​l​g\mathcal{Y}^{e,alg}_{\vec{\omega}} is the subset of 𝒴ω→e\mathcal{Y}^{e}_{\vec{\omega}} consisting of all Y∈𝒴ω→eY\in\mathcal{Y}^{e}_{\vec{\omega}} such that YY is algebraic.

Remark 6.2.

The algebraicity of 𝒴ω→\mathcal{Y}_{\vec{\omega}} depends only on ω→\vec{\omega} (Theorem 3.2), i.e. if ω→\vec{\omega} is algebraic, then all elements of 𝒴ω→\mathcal{Y}_{\vec{\omega}} are algebraic surfaces, and if ω→\vec{\omega} is not algebraic, then no element of 𝒴ω→\mathcal{Y}_{\vec{\omega}} is algebraic. Similarly, when ω→\vec{\omega} is essential, the algebraicity of ω→\vec{\omega} determines if 𝒴ω→e,a​l​g\mathcal{Y}^{e,alg}_{\vec{\omega}} is non-empty.

7. Canonical divisor

In this section we compute the canonical divisor of a primitive compactifications of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} in terms of the associated key sequence (Theorem 7.2), and give some of its applications. In section 7.1 we state Theorem 7.2 and use it to characterize ℙ2​(1,1,q)\mathbb{P}^{2}(1,1,q) in terms of log discrepancy and skewness of the curve at infinity. In section 7.2 we characterize when a primitive compactification has simple types of singularities or when it is Gorenstein. Finally, in section 7.3 we give the proof of Theorem 7.2.

7.1. The formula for canonical divisor and a characterization of ℙ2​(1,1,q)\mathbb{P}^{2}(1,1,q)

Let X:=ℂ2X:=\mathbb{C}^{2}. Throughout section 7.1 δ\delta is a divisorial semidegree on ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X].

Definition 7.1 ([Jon12, Section 9.3.3]).

Let X¯\bar{X} be a normal analytic compactification of XX such that δ\delta is centered at a curve CC at infinity on X¯\bar{X}. The log discrepancy AδA_{\delta} of δ\delta is one plus the coefficient of [C][C] in KX¯K_{\bar{X}} (where [C][C] is the Weil divisor corresponding to CC).

Let ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be the key sequence of δ\delta in some system of coordinates on XX. Then

7.2. Primitive compactifications with simple singularities

Throughout this section X¯\bar{X} is a primitive normal compactification of X:=ℂ2X:=\mathbb{C}^{2} and ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) is the key sequence corresponding to the semidegree δ\delta on ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X] with respect to a system of coordinates (x,y)(x,y) on XX such that δ⁡(x)>0\delta(x)>0. Assume X¯\bar{X} is algebraic. Then the sum of the geometric genera of singular points of X¯\bar{X} is equal to dimℂ(H0​(X¯,𝒪X¯​(KX¯))𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(H^{0}(\bar{X},\mathcal{O}_{\bar{X}}(K_{\bar{X}})).

Choose coordinates (x,y)(x,y) on XX such that the corresponding key sequence ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) of the semidegree on 𝕂⁡[x,y]\mathbb{K}[x,y] associated to C∞C_{\infty} is in the normal form. Following the characterization of Gorenstein primitive compactifications with rational singularities, we now characterize those with the next simplest type of singularities: we say that a primitive compactification X¯\bar{X} has a point with minimally elliptic singularity (in the sense of [Lau77]) if it is Gorenstein and has a point with elliptic singularity.

Definition 7.11.

Let q∈ℚq\in\mathbb{Q}, f∈ℂ⁡[u,v]f\in\mathbb{C}[u,v], and ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) be a Puiseux series in uu. We say that

  2. (2)

    ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) is a root exactly mod qq of f=0f=0 iff there exists a Puiseux series ϕ¯​(u)\bar{\phi}(u) such that f​(u,ϕ¯​(u))≡0f(u,\bar{\phi}(u))\equiv 0 and ϕ⁡(u)−ϕ¯​(u)=c​uq+h.o.t.\phi(u)-\bar{\phi}(u)=cu^{q}+\text{h.o.t.} for some c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C}, c≠0c\neq 0.

A mod qq root ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) of f=0f=0 has multiplicity mm iff there are exactly mm distinct Puiseux series ϕ¯1​(u),…,ϕ¯m​(u)\bar{\phi}_{1}(u),\ldots,\bar{\phi}_{m}(u) such that f⁡(u,ϕ¯k​(u))≡0f(u,\bar{\phi}_{k}(u))\equiv 0 and ϕ⁡(u)−ϕ¯k​(u)=ck​uq+h.o.t.\phi(u)-\bar{\phi}_{k}(u)=c_{k}u^{q}+\text{h.o.t.} for some ck∈ℂc_{k}\in\mathbb{C}, 1≤k≤m1\leq k\leq m. Similarly, ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) is an exactly mod qq root of multiplicity mm of f=0f=0 iff there are exactly mm distinct Puiseux series ϕ¯1​(u),…,ϕ¯m​(u)\bar{\phi}_{1}(u),\ldots,\bar{\phi}_{m}(u) which satisfy the conditions of the preceding sentence with ck≠0c_{k}\neq 0, 1≤k≤m1\leq k\leq m.

Remark 7.12.

Note that the notion of mod qq roots and exactly mod qq roots have (obvious) analogues in the case of descending Puiseux series: namely in Definition 7.11 replace every occurrence of ‘Puiseux series’ with ‘descending Puiseux series’, and ‘h.o.t.’ with ‘l.d.t.’, where as usual, l.d.t. stands for terms with lower degree (in uu).

Theorem 7.13 ([KP00, Theorem 1.1]).

Let q∈ℚ>0q\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0} and ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) be a Puiseux series which is a mod qq root of f=0f=0 of multiplicity m≥1m\geq 1. Then ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) is a mod qq root of ∂f/∂v=0\partial f/\partial v=0 of multiplicity m−1m-1.

Remark 7.14.

It was assumed throughout [KP00] that ff is mini-regular in vv, i.e. if d:=ord⁡(f)d:=\ord(f) then there is a monomial term in ff of the form c​vdcv^{d} with c∈ℂ∗c\in\mathbb{C}^{*}. However, the proof of Theorem 1.1 of [KP00] does not use this assumption.

Corollary 7.15.

Let g∈ℂ⁡[x,x−1,y]g\in\mathbb{C}[x,x^{-1},y] and ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) be a descending Puiseux series in xx which is a mod qq root of g=0g=0 of multiplicity m≥1m\geq 1. Then ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) is a mod qq root of ∂g/∂y=0\partial g/\partial y=0 of multiplicity m−1m-1.

Consider the (birational) change of coordinates (u,v)=(1/x,y/xd)(u,v)=(1/x,y/x^{d}), where d≫1d\gg 1. Let g~:=ud​degy​(g)​g​(1/u,v/ud)∈ℂ⁡[u,v]\tilde{g}:=u^{d\deg_{y}(g)}g(1/u,v/u^{d})\in\mathbb{C}[u,v]. Now note that y=ϕ⁡(x)y=\phi(x) is a mod qq root of g=0g=0 iff v=ud​ϕ​(1/u)v=u^{d}\phi(1/u) is a mod d−qd-q root of g~\tilde{g}. Theorem 7.13 implies that v=ud​ϕ​(1/u)v=u^{d}\phi(1/u) is a mod d−qd-q root of ∂g~/∂v\partial\tilde{g}/\partial v of multiplicity m−1m-1. Since ∂g~/∂v=ud⁡(degy⁡(g)−1)​∂g/∂y\partial\tilde{g}/\partial v=u^{d(\deg_{y}(g)-1)}\partial g/\partial y, it follows that y=ϕ⁡(x)y=\phi(x) is a mod qq root of ∂g/∂y=0\partial g/\partial y=0 of multiplicity m−1m-1, as required. ∎

Corollary 7.16.

Let f∈ℂ⁡[x,x−1,y]f\in\mathbb{C}[x,x^{-1},y] and ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) be a descending Puiseux series in xx. Let the multiplicity of ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) as a mod qq and exactly mod qq root of f=0f=0 be respectively m′m^{\prime} and mm (so that m′≥mm^{\prime}\geq m). Assume m′>m≥1m^{\prime}>m\geq 1. Then the multiplicity of ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) as an exactly mod qq root of ∂f/∂y=0\partial f/\partial y=0 is also mm.

Proof.

Let n:=m′−m≥1n:=m^{\prime}-m\geq 1. Then for all sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0, ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) is a mod (q−ϵ)(q-\epsilon) root of f=0f=0 of multiplicity nn, so that Corollary 7.15 implies that it is a mod (q−ϵ)(q-\epsilon) root of ∂f/∂y=0\partial f/\partial y=0 of multiplicity n−1n-1. On the other hand Corollary 7.15 also implies that ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) is a mod qq root of ∂f/∂y=0\partial f/\partial y=0 of multiplicity m′−1m^{\prime}-1. It follows that ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) is an exactly mod qq root of ∂f/∂y=0\partial f/\partial y=0 of multiplicity m′−1−(n−1)=mm^{\prime}-1-(n-1)=m. ∎

Appendix A Some properties of key forms

Let δ\delta be a divisorial semidegree such that δ⁡(x)>0\delta(x)>0, ϕ~δ​(x,ξ):=ϕδ​(x)+ξ​xrδ\tilde{\phi}_{\delta}(x,\xi):=\phi_{\delta}(x)+\xi x^{r_{\delta}} be the associated generic descending Puiseux series, g0=x,g1=y,…,gn+1g_{0}=x,g_{1}=y,\ldots,g_{n+1} be the corresponding sequence of key forms, and ω→:=(ω0,…,ωn+1)\vec{\omega}:=(\omega_{0},\ldots,\omega_{n+1}) be the key sequence. In this section we collect most of the properties of key forms used in this article. The assertions from A.1 and A.2 are used multiple times throughout the article; Corollary A.3 is used only in the proof of Proposition 5.1.

The following notations are used in this section: we denote the formal Puiseux pairs (resp. characteristic exponents) of ϕ~δ\tilde{\phi}_{\delta} by (q1,p1),…,(ql+1,pl+1)(q_{1},p_{1}),\ldots,(q_{l+1},p_{l+1}) (resp. χ1,…,χl+1\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{l+1}); recall that χj=qj/(p1⋯pj)\chi_{j}=q_{j}/(p_{1}\cdots p_{j}), 1≤j≤l+11\leq j\leq l+1. Also define α1,…,αn+1\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n+1} as in Definition 2.8.

Then

Proof.

algorithm 2.12 implies that

If β′\beta^{\prime} is key compatible with ϕ~\tilde{\phi}, then for all c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C}, the formal characteristic exponents of ϕ~+c​xβ′\tilde{\phi}+cx^{\beta^{\prime}} and ϕ~\tilde{\phi} are the same, so that the essential key sequences of the corresponding semidegrees are identical. Appendix C Effect of changes of coordinates on the generic descending Puiseux series of a semidegree

Theorem C.1 ([Jun42]).

Every polynomial automorphism FF of ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] has a factorization of the form

(57) F=Fk∘⋯∘F1\displaystyle F=F_{k}\circ\cdots\circ F_{1}

where each FjF_{j} is either an affine map of the form

(Type I) (u,v)↦(a​u+b​v+c,a′​u+b′​v+c′),a,b,c,a′,b′,c′∈ℂ\displaystyle(u,v)\mapsto(au+bv+c,a^{\prime}u+b^{\prime}v+c^{\prime}),\quad a,b,c,a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}

or a map of the form

(Type II) (u,v)↦(a​u+f⁡(v),b​v+c),a,b,c∈ℂ,f⁡(v)∈ℂ⁡[v]\displaystyle(u,v)\mapsto(au+f(v),bv+c),\quad a,b,c\in\mathbb{C},\ f(v)\in\mathbb{C}[v]

Let δ\delta be a semidegree on ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] such that δ⁡(x)>0\delta(x)>0. Let ϕ~δ​(x,ξ)\tilde{\phi}_{\delta}(x,\xi) be the generic descending Puiseux series of δ\delta in (x,y)(x,y) coordinates. For an automorphism FF of ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y], we write F∗​(ϕ~δ)F_{*}(\tilde{\phi}_{\delta}) for the generic descending Puiseux series of δ\delta after change of coordinates by FF; the precise definition is as follows.

Definition C.2.

Let F:ℂ⁡[x,y]→ℂ⁡[x,y]F:\mathbb{C}[x,y]\to\mathbb{C}[x,y] is an automorphism. Set (u,v):=(F⁡(x),F⁡(y))(u,v):=(F(x),F(y)). If δ⁡(u)>0\delta(u)>0, then construct the generic descending Puiseux series ψ⁡(u,ξ)\psi(u,\xi) of δ\delta in (u,v)(u,v) coordinates. The push forward of ϕ~δ\tilde{\phi}_{\delta} by FF is F∗​(ϕ~δ):=ψ⁡(u,ξ)|u=xF_{*}(\tilde{\phi}_{\delta}):=\psi(u,\xi)|_{u=x}.

Remark C.3.

F∗​(ϕ~δ)F_{*}(\tilde{\phi}_{\delta}) is defined only if δ⁡(F⁡(x))>0\delta(F(x))>0. Moreover, computing F∗​(ϕ~δ)F_{*}(\tilde{\phi}_{\delta}) is tantamount to the following procedure:

  1. (Step 1)

    convert the relation “y=ϕ~δ​(x,ξ)|ξ=λy=\tilde{\phi}_{\delta}(x,\xi)|_{\xi=\lambda}”, λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}, to a relation of the form “F⁡(y)=ψ~λ​(F⁡(x))F(y)=\tilde{\psi}_{\lambda}(F(x))”, where ψ~λ=∑βaβ′​xβ\tilde{\psi}_{\lambda}=\sum_{\beta}a^{\prime}_{\beta}x^{\beta} is a descending Puiseux series in xx.

  2. (Step 2)

    Take the highest exponent r′r^{\prime} of xx such that ar′′a^{\prime}_{r^{\prime}} is a non-constant function of λ\lambda. Then F∗​(ϕ~δ)=∑β>r′aβ′​xβ+ξ​xr′F_{*}(\tilde{\phi}_{\delta})=\sum_{\beta>r^{\prime}}a^{\prime}_{\beta}x^{\beta}+\xi x^{r^{\prime}}.

Lemma C.4.

  1. (1)

    Assume δ⁡(y)>0\delta(y)>0 and FF is the Type I automorphism (x,y)↦(y,x)(x,y)\mapsto(y,x). Then

    1. (a)

b=aω¯0​β​for all β such that aβ≠0.\displaystyle b=a^{\bar{\omega}_{0}\beta}\ \text{for all $\beta$ such that $a_{\beta}\neq 0$.}

In particular, b=aω¯1b=a^{\bar{\omega}_{1}}, which implies that F∈𝒢F\in\mathcal{G} in the case that ϕ\phi has only one monomial term, or equivalently, if n=1n=1. On the other hand if ϕ\phi has more than one monomial term, then it follows that aω¯0​β−ω¯1=1a^{\bar{\omega}_{0}\beta-\bar{\omega}_{1}}=1 for all β\beta such that aβ≠0a_{\beta}\neq 0. Theorem B.6 then implies that aa is an ω¯∗\bar{\omega}^{*}-th root of unity (ω¯∗\bar{\omega}^{*} being as in assertion 2), so that F∈𝒢F\in\mathcal{G} in this case as well. This completes the proof of assertion (2) of Theorem 4.9.
